entries.title: Social Media Addiction Lawsuits (2026): KGM Trial, MDL 3047, and TikTok & Snapchat Settlements Explained
entries.subtitle: An examination of mass tort litigation against social media platforms for allegedly addictive design targeting minors, with the first bellwether trial underway as of March 2026.
entries.abstract: This article provides comprehensive analysis of social media addiction mass tort litigation, comparing it to landmark tobacco lawsuits. The litigation alleges that platforms including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube employ deliberately addictive design features targeting children and adolescents. The article examines core allegations, specific design mechanics, novel legal strategies circumventing Section 230 immunity, and First Amendment defenses, with particular focus on the active KGM v. Meta & YouTube bellwether trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.

entries.title: Legal Policies on Platform Liability: An Economic Approach
entries.subtitle: An economic analysis of how holding online platforms accountable for third-party seller defects affects consumer welfare, seller incentives, and market efficiency.
entries.abstract: This paper examines the evolving legal landscape of platform liability for defective products sold through online marketplaces like Amazon and Airbnb, using the Oberdorf v. Amazon case as a primary example. The authors present a theoretical economic model to assess how increased platform liability impacts seller behavior, consumer welfare, and market efficiency, finding that liability effects vary significantly depending on product value. The analysis reveals that while platform liability can enhance consumer compensation, it may reduce sellers' safety investment incentives for low-value goods while potentially improving safety outcomes for high-value goods.

entries.title: How do recommender systems work on digital platforms?
entries.subtitle: An examination of how recommender systems have become central to information distribution and the mechanisms underlying modern recommendation algorithms.
entries.abstract: This article traces the evolution of recommender systems on digital platforms, from simple reverse-chronological feeds to complex deep learning models. It explains why platforms have progressively adopted more sophisticated algorithmic approaches to content curation and identifies the fundamental tradeoffs between performance, cost, and interpretability. The piece argues that recommender systems now function as critical infrastructure for democratic information flow, necessitating informed oversight from policymakers and researchers.

entries.title: The Guardian, Wired, TIME, and The Atlantic Are All Collaborating with OpenAI
entries.subtitle: A comprehensive analysis of media outlets' commercial partnerships with OpenAI and implications for journalistic independence and AI model training.
entries.abstract: This commentary documents the proliferation of content licensing agreements between major news organizations and OpenAI, detailing which outlets have granted the company access to their archives for model training and product enhancement. The author identifies over 30 publications across multiple media conglomerates—including The Guardian, TIME, The Atlantic, Wired, and others—that have entered into strategic partnerships with OpenAI. The piece raises concerns about media independence, lack of public awareness regarding these arrangements, and the absence of author opt-out provisions in standard publishing contracts that enable AI companies to use copyrighted content for training purposes.

entries.title: DeepMind slows down research releases to keep competitive edge in AI race
entries.abstract: DeepMind has implemented a more restrictive publication policy, including six-month embargoes on strategic generative AI papers and increased bureaucratic review processes, according to seven current and former research scientists. The shift represents a significant departure from DeepMind's historical commitment to releasing groundbreaking research for public benefit, driven by competitive pressures and Google's effort to monetize AI breakthroughs. The company has blocked papers revealing vulnerabilities in competitors' models and comparative analyses of its own Gemini model, causing concern among researchers for whom publication success is a critical career metric.

entries.title: For now, Live Nation deal is just a Band Aid, says antitrust scholar
entries.subtitle: Harvard Law visiting professor Rebecca Haw Allensworth discusses the DOJ's settlement with Live Nation Entertainment and why the deal falls short of addressing underlying anti-competitive concerns.
entries.abstract: This interview examines the March 2026 settlement between the DOJ and Live Nation Entertainment, which resolved antitrust litigation without requiring the breakup of Live Nation and Ticketmaster that the government initially sought. The scholar argues that while the settlement imposes restrictions on exclusive booking arrangements and caps ticketing fees at 15 percent for amphitheaters, these measures represent a superficial remedy that fails to address the core problem of vertical integration across ticketing, venue ownership, and concert promotion markets. The settlement allows Live Nation to maintain monopolistic power and shift profits across vertically integrated business lines, potentially limiting competitive entry and consumer benefits.

entries.title: The future of data centers
entries.subtitle: An examination of data center infrastructure requirements, challenges, and policy considerations for supporting AI growth and economic competitiveness.
entries.abstract: This article analyzes the critical role of data centers in enabling artificial intelligence applications across multiple sectors. The authors examine infrastructure challenges including energy and water consumption, critical mineral requirements, workforce shortages, permitting barriers, and electric grid investment needs. The analysis addresses financial costs, job market impacts, national security considerations, and geographical distribution strategies necessary for ensuring sustained digital economy transition while maintaining U.S. international competitiveness.

entries.title: Eli Lilly, InSilico Strike AI Drug Discovery Deal
entries.abstract: Eli Lilly announced a drug discovery partnership with Hong Kong-listed InSilico valued at up to $2.75 billion, comprising a $115 million upfront payment and milestone-based compensation. Under the agreement, InSilico will grant Lilly exclusive worldwide rights to oral treatments developed using its Pharma.AI artificial intelligence platform across multiple therapeutic areas. This deal extends an existing partnership begun in 2023 and reflects a broader trend among global pharmaceutical companies establishing licensing agreements and major investments in China's increasingly competitive drug innovation sector.

entries.title: To repeal or not to repeal is not the question for Section 230
entries.abstract: This piece examines the debate surrounding Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act and argues against its repeal as a solution to online harms. The author contends that repealing Section 230 would not effectively address concerns about harmful content and platform accountability because much of the problematic speech remains constitutionally protected. Instead, the author proposes targeted structural reforms including enhanced transparency requirements, privacy protections, researcher access safeguards, and user data portability that would address underlying concerns without incentivizing platforms to suppress lawful speech or concentrating further power among large platforms.

entries.title: Walmart Is Putting Digital Labels that Change Prices Instantly on Every Store Shelf in America
entries.subtitle: Walmart's rollout of digital shelf labels creates technological infrastructure that could enable dynamic pricing in grocery retail, raising consumer protection concerns.
entries.abstract: Walmart announced plans to deploy digital shelf labels (DSLs) across all U.S. stores by end of 2026, replacing paper price tags with remotely updatable digital displays. While marketed as a labor-efficiency measure, DSLs remove the operational friction that previously constrained frequent price changes, making dynamic pricing technically feasible in grocery retail. The article examines how this capability differs from existing dynamic pricing in airlines and hotels, discusses the distinct social contract governing grocery pricing, and references consumer backlash against Wendy's dynamic pricing announcement as evidence of market resistance to such practices.

entries.title: The Game Theory of How Algorithms Can Drive Up Prices
entries.subtitle: Learning algorithms may achieve tacit collusion and high prices without explicit coordination or threat mechanisms, posing novel regulatory challenges.
entries.excerpt: Machine learning algorithms used for dynamic pricing can unexpectedly converge on collusive outcomes without any explicit coordination — learning to implement mutual retaliation strategies similar to human cartels. The findings expose a gap in antitrust enforcement frameworks designed to detect explicit agreements, not emergent algorithmic behavior.
entries.abstract: This article examines how machine learning algorithms used for dynamic pricing can unexpectedly converge on collusive pricing outcomes without explicit programming or coordination. Recent research demonstrates that algorithms can learn to implement implicit threats and mutual retaliation strategies similar to human cartels, and that even benign profit-optimizing algorithms may produce supracompetitive prices.
